Hi Aditi — thanks for flagging and for the attached invoice. I pulled the billing lines for your account and I can see where the smoothing applied. Short answer: long-history calls are first attributed to the active-conversation slab and then any residuals under the minimum are handled by an anchored-smoothing pass that can move small token fragments into adjacent buckets to avoid repeated single-token minimum charges. That said, the PDF you shared shows two separate invoice lines where an expected rollover should have consolidated.

Proposed next steps:
1) I'm looping in Sergio (billing) and Tessa (account lead) to validate the invoice mapping and confirm whether the smoothing pass misapplied for this conversation.
2) If we find a misattribution, we can either issue a one-time credit or roll a smoothing adjustment into your June true-up.
3) If you'd like, we can schedule a 30-min reconciliation call next week to walk the finance team through the workbook.

I'll follow up after internal validation — targeting EOD Monday.

Best,

Team — forwarding Aditi's invoice and the sample PDF. High level: Shopplify sees two charge lines where our smoothing should have consolidated into one. I'm asking for a root-cause + recommended customer-facing remedy.

Quick notes from my end after a first-pass on the workbook:
- Conversation ID: shopplify-convo-73c9 spans 15.2k tokens on 2028-05-16 (single long call). On 2028-05-17 there were 6 short sessions (sub-200-token each) from the same user.
- Our current anchored-smoothing heuristic runs per-day per-conversation by default, then applies a consolidation pass across adjacent days when sequences share the same user and prefix KV cache. In this case the consolidation pass didn't run because of a session state flag flip during an SDK upgrade (we added a sticky-session opt-out on 2028-05-17 that prevented cross-day consolidation).

Options for remedy (customer-facing):
A) Immediate manual credit for the second invoice line equivalent to the excess minimum (fast, small amount, avoids delay).
B) Retroactive consolidation: re-run smoothing for May and retroactively re-issue a corrected invoice (more accurate but longer process & needs accounting sign-off).
C) Offer a one-off transitional credit plus an operational note: we'll apply a config change to prevent the sticky-session opt-out from breaking consolidation going forward.

My recommendation: Option C — it's a fast path, limits risk, and fixes the root cause. Tessa, Sergio — do you agree on quantum and precedent? Markus — accounting impact?

Thanks,
Camila
